chapters.s: The old people say there are three kinds of fear—the fear that comes upon the body, the fear that comes upon the house, and the fear that comes upon the name. A person may flee from the first two. The chapter ended on this question: when crime has moved out of paper, seals and warehouses and taken up residence in voices, numbers and phones, how many ears, how many registers and how much courage are needed to catch it? Chandrapal’s shadow is no longer…

The old people say trust is the oldest capital a village possesses. Even one who owns no field, no oxen and no ledger still owns trust. The chapter ended with the decision that the first way to break the seal on a voice is to share the voice. Madhukar is missing, Haricharan is uneasy, and Chandrapal’s “C. Babu” remains in shadow.…

People think dust is dirt. But in a record room dust is the oldest clerk of all. The chapter ended with the realization that traces of removed papers cannot be erased. Madhukar is missing, Haricharan absent, Parmanand half-broken, Nageshwar alive, and “17/C” stands like a new doorway.…

The old people say a net is recognised not by its mouth but by its belly. The mouth is different everywhere—here a voice on the phone, there a seal on a receipt, elsewhere the signboard of an office. That night the crocodile did not appear on the riverbank, but circular whirlpools kept rising in the water. The old client said, “The belly is inside.” Surmani Devi replied, “Now we are measuring the belly.” With that sentence the chapter ends.…
chapters.g: Aruni wrote: “Fear that the name will be removed, fear that the pension will stop, fear of being declared dead—three ropes.” Devika added: “The hand holding the ropes: the C-room.” Ananya wrote a third line: “The C-room is not merely a room; it is the belly of the net.” Reading it, Mira said, “That is the name of this chapter.”

chapters.s: Once the shadow has been caught, the question rises—where is the body? And a body is always found in some storehouse or granary. The chapter pauses here. Chandrapal’s shadow gave them a road toward the body; from the C-room to the C-17 box, from Madhukar’s receipt to the C Warehouse, from Dharni Mahato to Tetari Ghat, and from paper fibres to the darkness of the river.…

There is no scrap in the storehouse—what rots there is fear kept under lock. Grain shut away for a year merely grows old; fear shut away for a year swells until it fills the boxes, and its smell tears through the lock and escapes. The chapter ends here. The storehouse at Imli Ghat proved to hold not scrap but a warehouse of fear, papers, voices and preparations for death. The C-17 box, five red ledgers, voice rehearsals, the list of elderly people’s circumstances, and “next consignment…

The voice is made across the river, but it is the people on this bank who drown. The current separates the two villages, so people think the far bank is distant. The chapter ends here. Tetari Ghat’s “new voice list” has been traced to the Public Service Centre across the river. Counterfeit captivity through voice, lists of elderly people’s circumstances, theft of family rhythms…

The old people say no village name walks to the city on its own feet. Someone carries it—sometimes in a form, sometimes in a receipt, sometimes in a free scan, sometimes in the hands of someone who speaks sweetly and says, “I’ll clean up the system for you.” And once a name travels out… The chapter ends with this understanding: the city’s throat has been caught, but its true larynx has not yet been fully exposed. The village name travelled to the city through public service, registers, pensions, banks, and lawsuits…

The old people say that adding a number to a name is one of the oldest tricks. Chandra One, Chandra Two—the moment a number is added, the name becomes half one’s own and half someone else’s. From the Chandra Service Office came the Old Trust List, emotional signals, institutional voices, and the shadow of Chandra 1. The marketplace of digital fear now reached directly into old court cases, land disputes, pensions, migrant sons…

The old people say some names grow larger than their bodies. Such names sometimes do more work after death than while alive, because a living person can be questioned and a name cannot. Here the first great circle of digital fear closes. Chandra 2 was an office; Chandra 1 was a mask of voice. Mohanlal Jha’s room, samples of old speeches, the Father and Officer pen drives…

chapters.t: The Invisible Court of Channa Grove
chapters.s: The old people say every village has two courts—one with walls, and one with only ears. In the first, dates are fixed; in the second, words are laid down. The first day of this invisible court ends here. People left behind knots of their fear, while Madhukar Babu’s shadow was now moving in a definite direction.

The old people say there is only one rule for opening a knot—do not jerk it. If thread is pulled with a jerk, the knot tightens; and if a person’s fear is struck with a jerk, it retreats inside again, and the second time it may not come out. This section ends with the reading of the knots. The invisible court has moved from emotion toward method. The first written thread leading to Madhukar Mishra has been found, but with that thread a new danger is born…

The elders say that the most dangerous list is not the one marked “Punishment.” The most dangerous list is the one marked “Assistance.” People hide a punishment list, but they make an assistance list with their own hands—writing down their widows, their old people, their sons away from home… By dawn the register had survived. The original page was safe, the copies were safe, the note was safe, and the watchers were tired but upright. When the first morning light fell through the window onto the page…

chapters.t: The Threshold of the Invisible Court
chapters.s: The elders say that people take off their shoes of their own accord where they believe their words will be heard. Why do people remove their shoes in a temple? And that night the wind opened the first page of the notebook Clerk Ramballabh had left on the stone. Among the names written there was one that, when heard, would make the breath of the old wrongdoing stop—the actual seal-bearer of Batuknath Hariharan.…

The name Dinbandhu that rose from Ramballabh’s notebook was not the name of one man alone; with it came a cloth bag, red wax, a brass seal and the rustle of blank papers. “Seal-bearer” sounds like a small task, but the door of trust opens and closes through that hand. And before dawn the wind opened one page of Dinbandhu’s diary. Only two words were clear on it: “Final List.” Beneath was a date from the same week in which, at Batuknath Hariharan’s service ceremony…

The final list is written on the smallest page, yet casts the largest shadow. Names fit on a small sheet, but the bodies behind the names, the fields, the sweat, a child’s hunger and the hopes of old parents do not. The invisible court gave no verdict that night. But the cloth from the service ceremony, Dinbandhu’s slip, the testimony of the women’s line and the words “change the original” became so heavy together that the stump’s shadow seemed pressed into the earth.…

A threshold is the first boundary of truth. Opening the box inside may be easy, but evidence found in a box opened without permission is itself stained by injustice. In the final watch, Ragini Devi’s page, the line on Lalit’s poster, Chamru’s four names and Shanti’s “assistance spoken, consent written” were placed upon the cloth.…

The stairs do not take justice upward; they take it inward. On every step rests not merely the weight of a foot but years of silence. At last Satyavrat Mehta said, “The upper room has opened. Now we must open the road above it—the tehsil, the bank, the register, the city office.” The children opened the next page of the register.…

A step... a step is not merely the mark of a foot; it is the account of trust travelling from one place to another. A shawl was offered on a village stage, rights disappeared into a tehsil register, a photograph lodged in a city archive, and a bank account divided the money along three paths. The seals from the upper room were no longer merely footprints; they had become a road. The road the offenders had built in silence would now be walked by the child sentinels of names, lamps in their hands.

The city’s account joins land, loans, charity, phones and stolen identity into one chain of evidence. Aruni and Ananya learn that a false name or borrowed face does not erase time, place, device or message; identifying the ‘teeth of the digital crocodile’ opens the next stage of the investigation.
